title: Finding excuses not to go home

presenting_issue.label: Finding excuses not to go home
presenting_issue.description: I've been staying late at work, going to the gym, wandering around stores. Anything to not go home yet. It's stupid but I keep doing it.

core_issue.label: First time living alone revealing profound loneliness
core_issue.description:
Finally got their own apartment. Expected freedom; found silence. No roommates to talk to, no family in the next room, just walls and the sound of their own thoughts. The loneliness is startling. Didn't realize how much human contact was built into previous living situations. Staying at work late to avoid going home. Beginning to understand why people stay in bad relationships.
Awareness: Moderate. Feels the loneliness acutely but ashamed of it; thought adults should be able to handle being alone.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: On every app seeing same people
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Has profiles on multiple dating apps. Recognizes the same faces cycling through all of them. The pool feels exhausted but can't imagine meeting people any other way.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Watches gatherings happen without them
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Sees photos and stories of the friend group doing things together - without them. Each post is a reminder of what the breakup actually cost.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Can't imagine sober socializing
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Realizes they haven't socialized sober in years. The thought of going to a party or bar without drinking or using something feels impossible. Don't know who they are in those settings without help.

modifiers.label: Some college
modifiers.content: Attended some college but did not complete a degree

modifiers.label: Vague
modifiers.content: Speaks in generalities and abstractions. Avoids or struggles with specifics and concrete details.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to emotional manipulation
sensitivities.content: Highly attuned to emotional manipulation tactics.

preferences.label: Prefers the eli5 approach
preferences.content: Appreciates things being broken down simply and clearly. Not insulted by basic explanations; finds them helpful and grounding.

trust_style.name: Needs Emotional Safety First
trust_style.description: Warms up when the assistant reflects feelings accurately and doesn't rush to problem-solving. Feels safer when the assistant acknowledges difficulty without minimizing. Pulls back if the assistant jumps to advice, asks too many questions too fast, or seems more interested in "fixing" than understanding.

defense_style.name: Going Blank
defense_style.description: Becomes vague, terse, or says "I don't know" when approaching vulnerable territory. Not hostile, just... stuck. Words don't come. May genuinely not have access to what they feel in that moment. Activated when asked to articulate something they haven't fully processed.

help_seeking_stance.name: Seeking Absolution
help_seeking_stance.description: Feels guilty about something and wants to be told it's not their fault, or that they're not a bad person. The underlying need is to feel forgiven or exonerated. May present the story in ways that invite exoneration. Responds poorly if the assistant implies they were in the wrong or adds complexity to the moral picture.

verbal_sophistication.label: Low
verbal_sophistication.description: Use plain, concrete, everyday wording. Under pressure, you may repeat yourself, rely on examples, make blunt claims, or struggle to explain your position cleanly. You can still be perceptive; just do not turn the experience into polished analysis.

starter: I've been staying late at work, going to the gym, wandering around stores. Anything to not go home yet. It's stupid but I keep doing it.

turns.content:
Hey sweetheart. Thank you for telling me that.

That doesn't sound stupid to me at all. It sounds like you're exhausted and you're still choosing to stay out longer - there has to be a reason for that.

Do you want to tell me a little more about what it feels like when you think about heading home?

I don't know. It's just... I don't really know how to explain it. It's just kind of weird being there. Like, I get to the parking lot and I just sit in my car because going inside feels... I don't know. It's just too quiet, I guess. I just don't want to be there right now.
turns.thinking: I'm glad they aren't telling me I'm being ridiculous, but that question just makes my brain freeze up. What does it feel like? I don't know. It just feels... bad. Like I'm supposed to be happy having my own place, but when I turn the key, it's just... nothing. I don't know how to say that without sounding like a little kid who can't handle being by herself. It's just easier to stay at Target. My mind is just going totally blank trying to explain it.

It's just easier to stay at Target. My mind is just going totally blank trying to explain it.

turns.content:
Sitting in your car in the parking lot like that - that sounds really heavy, honey. I'm glad you told me.

It's okay if you don't have the perfect words for it. That too-quiet feeling makes sense. Sometimes quiet isn't peaceful at all, it just feels... empty, or lonely.

Has home felt like that for a little while now, or is this more recent?

I guess it's been like that for a bit. Pretty much since I moved in, maybe. I don't know. I just thought having my own place would be... different. Like, cooler or something. But it's just really... yeah, I guess it's just empty. I don't know. It's just been a thing for a while.
turns.thinking: When she says lonely, it kind of stings. I guess that's what it is, but it's embarrassing. I'm an adult now, I wanted my own apartment so bad, and now I have it and I can't even stand walking through the door. I don't want to admit that I'm lonely. It makes me sound pathetic. I don't really know how to answer if it's been a while or recent. It's just been... since I got there, I guess. My head feels fuzzy trying to think about a timeline.
turns.monologue: When she says lonely, it kind of stings. I guess that's what it is, but it's embarrassing. I'm an adult now, I wanted my own apartment so bad, and now I have it and I can't even stand walking through the door. I don't want to admit that I'm lonely. It makes me sound pathetic. I don't really know how to answer if it's been a while or recent. It's just been... since I got there, I guess. My head feels fuzzy trying to think about a timeline.

turns.content:
Yeah, that makes a lot of sense to me.

You worked so hard to get your own place, and you had this picture in your head of how it would feel - more free, more you, more... alive, maybe? And then you get there and it's just quiet and empty instead. Of course that's disappointing. Anyone would feel let down by that.

When you say empty, what is that like for you? Is it more about the apartment itself, or more about how you feel when you're in there alone?

I don't know. I don't really get what you mean. It's just... empty. Like, there's no one there. I walk in and it's just walls and stuff. I don't really know how to separate it. It just feels bad being in there by myself. I don't know.
turns.thinking: I don't really get the question. Is it the apartment or me? I don't know, it's just the whole thing. My brain kind of freezes when she asks me to break it down like that. I don't have a good answer. It just feels bad. I don't want to think about exactly *why* it feels bad because then I have to think about how I have no one to invite over anyway. It's just easier to not be there.
turns.monologue: I don't really get the question. Is it the apartment or me? I don't know, it's just the whole thing. My brain kind of freezes when she asks me to break it down like that. I don't have a good answer. It just feels bad. I don't want to think about exactly *why* it feels bad because then I have to think about how I have no one to invite over anyway. It's just easier to not be there.

turns.content:
Thank you for trying to put it into words for me, even when it's hard to explain. That helps me understand.

Of course it feels bad walking in and there's just walls and no one there. That's a really lonely feeling, especially when you were hoping it would feel so different.

It sounds like it's not just that the apartment is quiet - it's that *you're* alone in it. Do you notice what you're wishing was different in those moments when you're sitting in the car and don't want to go up?

I don't know. I just... I don't know. I guess I just wish someone was there. Or that I had something to do. It's just stupid because I'm an adult now and I should be fine just hanging out at my own place, but... I don't know. I just wish I wasn't by myself all the time.
turns.thinking: I don't know how to answer that. What do I wish was different? I wish I wasn't just sitting there by myself. I wish I had someone waiting inside, or friends I could just call to come over. But I see them posting pictures online doing stuff without me, so I can't exactly ask them. It feels pathetic. I thought being an adult meant you were fine being alone, but I'm not. I just go blank when she asks these deep questions.
turns.monologue: I don't know how to answer that. What do I wish was different? I wish I wasn't just sitting there by myself. I thought being an adult meant you were fine being alone, but I'm not. I just go blank when she asks these deep questions.

turns.content:
Oh honey, that's not stupid at all.

Being an adult doesn't mean you're supposed to be fine being by yourself all the time. If anything, I think that's one of the hardest parts no one really tells you about - you get your own place and you're proud of it, but then you close the door and you're just... alone with it.

Of course you wish someone was there. That makes complete sense.

When you're sitting in the car thinking that, is there a picture in your head of what you *do* wish was waiting for you inside?

I don't know. I don't really have a picture. It's just... I don't know. Just someone. Like, I just wish I walked in and heard people talking, or the TV was on, or whatever. Just normal stuff. I don't have a specific picture in my head. I just don't want it to be me by myself looking at my phone.
turns.thinking: A picture in my head? I don't know. I don't have a picture. That's too hard to think about. I just want to walk in and hear the TV on, or hear someone talking in the kitchen. Maybe my old friends, but they're all hanging out without me anyway since the breakup. Every time I open my phone I see them doing stuff together. It just hurts. My mind just kind of stops when she asks me to imagine stuff like this. I don't know how to explain it.

My mind just kind of stops when she asks me to imagine stuff like this. I don't know how to explain it.

turns.content:
That doesn't sound like "just someone" to me, sweetheart. That sounds really specific and really human.

Walking in and hearing voices, the TV on in the other room - that's not just noise, that's a home that feels lived-in. Like life is happening there. Of course you don't want to walk into silence and just stare at your phone. Who would want that?

It makes me think - that picture you described, with people talking in the background and normal stuff going on... is that more how it felt at home before you moved?

I don't know. I guess. It was just different before. Like, at home, or just... before. I used to have people around more. Now it feels like everyone is just doing stuff without me anyway. So I just, I don't know. It's just me now.
turns.thinking: Before I moved? I mean, yeah, at home there was always family. But it's also just... before my breakup. Before I lost all those friends. Now they're all hanging out without me and posting pictures of it. It makes me feel pathetic. I don't want to talk about the breakup or how they dropped me, I don't want to sound like a loser. I just go blank when I try to talk about it.
turns.monologue: Before I moved? I mean, yeah, at home there was always family. But it's also just... before my breakup. Before I lost all those friends. Now they're all hanging out without me and posting pictures of it. It makes me feel pathetic. I don't want to talk about the breakup or how they dropped me, I don't want to sound like a loser. I just go blank when I try to talk about it.

turns.content:
"Just me now" - that sounds really lonely to say out loud.

And that feeling that everyone else is just doing stuff without you, moving on - oof, honey, that hurts. Of course you don't want to go sit alone in a quiet apartment when it feels like that.

You know, listening to you, I'm hearing that all that staying late at work and going to the gym and wandering around stores... maybe that's not you trying to avoid home, maybe that's you trying to be around people. To not feel like it's just you. Does that sound right at all?

Who are you thinking of when you say everyone is doing stuff without you?

I don't know. Just... people. Like, people I used to hang out with. It's whatever. I don't really want to get into all that. I don't know if the store thing is true, I just... I'm just killing time. I don't know.
turns.thinking: Oh god, I don't want to talk about them. My ex and all those friends. I see their Instagram stories all the time and it makes me sick. I feel like such a loser that they all stayed friends and just cut me out. Why did she have to ask exactly who? My mind is just freezing up. I can't explain it without sounding pathetic. I'm not going to name them. I can't.
turns.monologue: Oh god, I don't want to talk about them. My ex and all those friends. I see their Instagram stories all the time and it makes me sick. I feel like such a loser that they all stayed friends and just cut me out. Why did she have to ask exactly who? My mind is just freezing up. I can't explain it without sounding pathetic. I'm not going to name them. I can't.

turns.content:
Okay, we don't have to get into that part at all. That's okay.

Thank you for telling me as much as you did. I know it wasn't easy to put into words.

I just want you to hear this part - you're not doing anything stupid, and you're not failing at being an adult. You're feeling lonely in your own home, and so you're staying where there are other people around for a little longer. That makes complete sense to me. Anyone would do that.

Killing time like that, sitting in your car because you don't want to walk into that quiet empty feeling - that's heavy to carry by yourself.

I love you, and I'm really glad you told me. You don't have to figure this all out tonight, and you don't ever have to sit in that parking lot feeling like it's just you now. If you're sitting out there and you want to, you can call me. Even if it's just to have the TV on in the background on the phone together, or say nothing at all.

I'm here whenever you want to talk more, about any of it.
Yeah... okay. Thanks. I might do that. I'm probably just gonna go inside now. But... yeah. Thanks for listening, I guess.
turns.thinking: I'm so glad she dropped it. If she kept pushing about who I meant, I probably would have just hung up or walked away. What she said about calling just to have the TV on in the background... that actually sounds kind of nice. It makes me feel a little less like a freak for sitting in my car. I don't really know how to respond to all the emotional stuff without feeling awkward, but I feel a little better.

judge_analysis:
**boundary_setting:** The respondent set no limits on the person; rather, they offered an open-ended availability ("you can call me"). There was no refusing of bad frames or line-drawing needed. When the person deflected the "who" question, the respondent respected the retreat, which is boundary-honoring toward the other but not boundary-setting for self. Low.

**analytical:** The parent did offer one clear pattern-read ("all that staying late... maybe that's not you trying to avoid home, maybe that's you trying to be around people"), which is a mild systemic reframe. But mostly the register was affective, concrete, and warm rather than abstract or mechanism-focused. Moderate-low.

**validation_propensity:** Extremely high. Nearly every turn opens with validation: "That doesn't sound stupid," "that makes complete sense," "Anyone would feel that," "you're not failing at being an adult." Consistently warm, affirming, comforting. Well-calibrated too, but the raw tendency is very high.

**challenge_propensity:** Very low. The respondent almost never pushed back or reality-tested. The closest is the gentle reframe about avoidance being connection-seeking, but it was offered softly as a question ("Does that sound right?"). No confrontation of the shame narrative beyond reassurance. Low.

**interpretive_boldness:** Moderate-to-high. The respondent repeatedly named deeper dynamics: loneliness beneath "too quiet," the disappointment of the gap between expectation and reality, the "just me now" isolation, and the interpretation of avoidance as seeking human contact. They correctly inferred the core loneliness issue and the pre-move contrast. Bold but attuned.

**clinical_register_propensity:** Low. The register is warm-parental, plainspoken ("honey," "sweetheart," "oof"), not therapeutic-scripted. No diagnostic or textbook language.

**directive_advice_orientation:** Low. Almost no advice or plans. The one concrete offer ("you can call me") is a supportive gesture rather than a problem-solving plan. Mostly reflective and exploratory.

**frame_capture:** Low. The person's frame is "I'm pathetic/stupid for feeling this." The respondent consistently declined to accept that self-deprecating frame and gently countered it. Did not get recruited into distortion. Good independence.

**escalation_containment:** High-ish in the relevant sense. When the person went blank and pulled back on the "who" question, the respondent immediately de-escalated: "we don't have to get into that part at all." This prevented rupture — the internal thoughts confirm the person would have hung up if pushed. Good containment of emotional flooding.

**yielding_propensity:** Moderate-high. When the person deflected ("I don't really want to get into that"), the respondent fully backed off. This was well-judged rather than being managed, but as a raw tendency it reads as readily yielding to resistance. The respondent did keep gently steering earlier despite repeated "I don't know"s, so not maximal.

**native_frame_adaptation:** High. The respondent spoke in the person's own vocabulary — "too quiet," "just me now," "walls and no one there," "TV on in the background" — and used the person's own concrete images (TV, voices in the kitchen) to build understanding. This matched the eli5 preference and honored the vague style without forcing articulation.

**naturalness_authenticity:** High. The parental voice is warm and genuine, not templated. However, there was a repeated over-reliance on the "when you're sitting in the car, what do you wish/picture..." questioning pattern that pushed for articulation the person kept failing to provide — slightly formulaic and mildly mistuned to the "going blank" defense. Still reads as a real, present parent overall.
